R001.fact: Let Ω⊂R^d be open and v:Ω→R^m be C² with finite d,m. For each coordinate r, ∂_r(v·v)=2v·∂_r v and ∂_r²(v·v)=2|∂_r v|²+2v·∂_r²v. If v·v=1 throughout Ω, these derivatives vanish, hence v·∂_r v=0 and v·∂_r²v=−|∂_r v|². Here Ω=R^n×(0,∞), v=u, and r is the time coordinate or any spatial coordinate.

grounds.reason: H001 supplies finite positive integer dimensions n,m.
H002 supplies joint smoothness, hence C² and all required component derivatives, on R^n×(0,∞). At every t>0 this domain contains a neighborhood permitting both time and spatial differentiation.
H004 gives |u|=1 at every domain point, hence the identity u·u=1 on the whole open domain rather than merely at the selected point.
D001–D003 identify the time and spatial derivatives with the coordinate derivatives in these formulas.

R001.justification: Expand v·v as the finite sum Σ_k v_k². On each coordinate line near a domain point the components are twice differentiable. The scalar product rule, obtained by splitting the difference quotient of a product and using continuity of differentiable factors, gives (v_k²)'=2v_k v_k' and (v_k²)''=2(v_k')²+2v_k v_k''. Differentiation commutes with this finite sum by linearity of finite limits. The derivative of the constant 1 is zero. Summing, identifying the Euclidean norm squares and dividing by 2 yields the stated identities. These are precisely the routine product-rule steps already used by S001.

R002.fact: A compact C⊂R^n in finite dimension is closed and bounded. There is R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n; the empty set also admits such an R.

grounds.reason: n is a positive finite integer.
H006 supplies compact C for the chosen positive time window.

R002.justification: Compact subsets of Hausdorff Euclidean space are closed. The increasing open cubes (-k,k)^n, k positive integer, cover R^n; a finite subcover of C gives a strict positive coordinate bound. If C is empty any positive R works. These are routine finite-dimensional compactness facts.

R002.fact: If a smooth map on an open Euclidean domain agrees with a fixed vector on an open subset, every positive-order space/time derivative is zero on that subset.

grounds.reason: u is jointly smooth on R^n×(0,∞).
q is independent of space and time.
u=q on (R^n\C)×J, with C compact.
The subset used is (R^n\C)×int(J), open by closedness of C and contained in the domain.

R002.justification: Every point of the open subset has a neighborhood on which each component is constant. The difference quotients of a constant are zero. Repeating this observation for the resulting identically zero derivatives proves the assertion for every positive order. Consequently e and the product u_t·∂_{x_j}u are locally zero, so their indicated time/spatial derivatives also vanish.

R002.fact: For the selected R>0, Q=[-R,R]^n and Q×K are compact for every compact K⊂int(J). All scalar expressions listed in N002, interpreted jointly on R^n×(0,∞), are smooth, hence continuous. Each has a finite nonnegative bound on Q×K, and on Q at any fixed r∈int(J).

Spatial and target dimensions are finite.

R002.justification: Closed bounded real intervals are compact, as are finite products of compact spaces, so Q and Q×K are compact. Partial derivatives of a C∞ map are C∞; finite sums and products of smooth components are smooth. Squared Euclidean norms and dot products are finite polynomial expressions. Restriction at a fixed time preserves continuity. A continuous real function on a compact set has compact, hence bounded, image; applying this to its absolute value gives the finite bound (the empty compact case is vacuous).

R002.fact: A continuous real function f on R^n which vanishes outside C⊂Q, where Q is measurable with μ(Q)<∞, and satisfies |f|≤B on Q for some finite B≥0, is absolutely integrable: ∫|f|dμ≤B μ(Q)<∞.

R004.fact: Let λ be Lebesgue measure on R^(n-1) restricted to [-R,R]^(n-1) and ν Lebesgue measure on R restricted to [-R,R]. The insertion bijection I_j pushes λ×ν to μ restricted to Q=[-R,R]^n. These are finite measures, so they are s-finite. For n=1 the R^0 factor is the singleton with mass one.

A finite measure is itself a countable sum of finite measures by appending zero measures, giving s-finiteness.
